mainTopic: Which grade of land creditors collect from: how land is graded, עולא's תקנה for lenders, and collecting from buyers of the debtor's fields.
overview: The amud opens by finishing a ברייתא that lists which grade of land each claimant collects from. The גמרא uses its middle clause to challenge the view that land is graded against the owner's own fields (בשלו הן שמין). It answers that the case is one where the borrower once owned עידית and sold it, and רב חסדא says the same. A second ברייתא seems to contradict the first, and the גמרא settles the clash in four ways. These are: רב חסדא's case, whether his בינונית matches the world's עידית, a dispute between בשלו and בשל עולם, and רבינא's view that the תנאים disagree about עולא's teaching. עולא teaches that by Torah law a בעל חוב collects from זיבורית, but the Sages gave him בינונית so that people would keep lending. Then a new ברייתא covers a debtor who sold his fields. Buyers who bought from him take his place, but when there were several buyers one after the other, creditors collect from the last buyer first. The גמרא explains why a single buyer is different. He bought the עידית last, and he can threaten to return the זיבורית to the seller. It then begins a new challenge that continues on the next amud.

steps.title: End of the ברייתא: owner of only best and worst land
steps.stepSummary: The last part of the ברייתא being quoted: if he owns only עידית and זיבורית, damages are paid from the עידית, and a בעל חוב and a כתובה are paid from the זיבורית.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he has only top-quality and low-quality land, damages are paid from the top-quality land. A creditor and a wife's כתובה are paid from the low-quality land.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing its quote of a ברייתא that it brought as a challenge. This step only sets up the source; the actual challenge comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא has a standard ranking: נזיקין collect from the best land, a בעל חוב from the middle land, and a כתובה from the worst land. This clause covers someone who has no middle land at all. Here the בעל חוב drops down to the זיבורית together with the כתובה.

keyTerms.meaning: The money a wife is owed through her marriage contract

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a new ברייתא. It is the tail end of a ברייתא the גמרא started quoting right before this, and the challenge built from it comes in the next step.

phrases.english: If he has top-quality and low-quality land,
phrases.notes: He has no middle-quality land at all.

phrases.english: damages are paid from the top-quality land,
and a creditor and a woman's כתובה are paid from the low-quality land.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the ברייתא the גמרא began quoting just before, as a challenge to בשלו הן שמין.
steps.kashyaTarget: The view that land is graded relative to the payer's own fields (בשלו הן שמין).
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: This step only finishes quoting the source; the attack itself is spelled out in step 2.

steps.title: The middle clause challenges grading by his own land
steps.stepSummary: The middle clause says that a בעל חוב collects from the בינונית when there is only בינונית and זיבורית. If land were graded by his own fields, that בינונית would count as his עידית, and the בעל חוב should be sent to the זיבורית.
steps.simpleTranslation: Look at the middle clause: if he has middle and low land, damages and the creditor are paid from the middle land, and the כתובה from the low land. But if we grade by his own land, his middle land should count as top land, and the creditor should be pushed to the low land!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points to the middle clause of the ברייתא and uses it to attack the view of בשלו הן שמין.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Under בשלו הן שמין, the best field a person owns counts as his עידית. If he owns only middle and low land, his middle land becomes his 'best,' and a בעל חוב should not collect from it. Yet the ברייתא lets the בעל חוב collect from it, which suggests land is graded by general market standards (בשל עולם).

keyTerms.meaning: Land is graded by comparing it to the owner's own other fields
He should be pushed off to

steps.confusionAlert: 'Graded by his own land' means comparing his fields to each other, not to what land is worth in the general market. Under that view, a person's best field is always his עידית, even if it is average by market standards.

phrases.english: In any case, it teaches in the middle clause:
If he has middle-quality and low-quality land,
damages and a creditor are paid from the middle-quality land,
and a woman's כתובה from the low-quality land.
Now if you say they grade by his own land,
let his middle-quality land be treated as top-quality land,
and the creditor should be pushed off to the low-quality land!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the actual challenge out of the ברייתא quoted in step 1.
steps.kashyaTarget: The view of בשלו הן שמין.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Under that view, his בינונית would count as his עידית, so a בעל חוב should not collect from it. The ברייתא says he does collect from it, so grading must be by market standards.

steps.title: He once owned top land and sold it
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the ברייתא is talking about someone who owned עידית when he took the loan and sold it later.
steps.simpleTranslation: What case are we dealing with here? A case where he had top-quality land and sold it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends בשלו הן שמין by placing the ברייתא in a specific case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A creditor's claim on the land takes hold when the loan is made. At that time the borrower still owned his עידית, so his middle field really was his בינונית even by his own standards. Selling the עידית later does not change the grade that was set when the loan was made, so the בעל חוב collects from the בינונית.

keyTerms.meaning: What case are we dealing with here? (used to narrow a source to a specific case)
For example; such as a case where

steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא does not prove בשל עולם הן שמין. It can be explained as a case where the borrower owned עידית when the loan was made and sold it afterward.

phrases.english: What case are we dealing with here?
A case where he had top-quality land, and he sold it.
phrases.notes: He owned it when he took the loan and sold it afterward.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 2.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the ברייתא to a specific case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא seemed to show that a person's best field is not automatically graded as his עידית, which would mean grading is by market standards.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא is a case where he once owned עידית. When the loan was made, his middle field was truly his בינונית, so בשלו הן שמין still stands.

steps.title: רב חסדא says the same answer
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא is quoted giving the very same explanation: the case is one where he had עידית and sold it.
steps.simpleTranslation: And so said רב חסדא: it is a case where he had top-quality land and sold it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא backs up its answer by showing that the אמורא רב חסדא explained the ברייתא the same way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nothing new is added to the logic. The answer in step 3 is now supported by a named authority, which shows it is an accepted explanation and not just a forced answer to escape the challenge.

keyTerms.meaning: And so said (introduces support for what was just said)

phrases.english: And so said רב חסדא:
A case where he had top-quality land, and he sold it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the answer of step 3 with the same statement from רב חסדא.
steps.raayaObject: The answer that the ברייתא is a case where he owned עידית and sold it.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A statement of רב חסדא saying exactly the same thing.

steps.title: Another ברייתא seems to contradict the first one
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says רב חסדא's explanation makes sense, and brings a second ברייתא. In that ברייתא, when there is only בינונית and זיבורית, the בעל חוב collects from the זיבורית. That clashes with the first ברייתא.
steps.simpleTranslation: This also makes sense, because another ברייתא teaches: if he has בינונית and זיבורית, damages come from the בינונית, while a creditor and a woman's כתובה come from the זיבורית. The two ברייתות contradict each other!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up a proof for רב חסדא. It quotes a second ברייתא that seems to clash with the first one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first ברייתא lets the בעל חוב take בינונית when the debtor has only בינונית and זיבורית. The second ברייתא, in the very same situation, sends him to the זיבורית. Something must explain the difference, and the next step will say what.

keyTerms.meaning: This also makes sense; an opening line that brings support for what was just said
The money a wife is owed from her husband under her marriage contract

phrases.english: This too makes sense,
phrases.notes: "This" means רב חסדא's explanation from the last step: he had עידית and sold it.

phrases.english: since another ברייתא teaches:
If he has middle-quality and poor-quality land,
damages are paid from the middle-quality land,
a creditor and a woman's marriage contract are paid from the poor-quality land.
They contradict each other!
phrases.notes: The first ברייתא gave the creditor the middle-quality land in this same situation.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a second ברייתא to back up רב חסדא's explanation.
steps.raayaObject: רב חסדא's explanation that the first ברייתא is about someone who had עידית and sold it.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A second ברייתא that sends the בעל חוב to the זיבורית when the debtor has only בינונית and זיבורית.

steps.title: The contradiction is settled only by רב חסדא's case
steps.stepSummary: The only way to make the two ברייתות fit is to say the first is about a man who had עידית and sold it, and the second is about a man who never had עידית.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, must we not learn from this: here, it is where he had עידית and sold it; there, it is where he did not have עידית and sell it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the proof. The contradiction disappears once you use רב חסדא's explanation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If he once had עידית, his בינונית really is middle-quality, so the בעל חוב can collect from it. If he never had עידית, his בינונית is his best land and counts as his עידית, so the בעל חוב goes to the זיבורית. Since this split explains both ברייתות, רב חסדא's reading is supported.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, must we not learn from this...? A way of drawing a conclusion
Here... there; splitting two sources into two different cases

steps.whatToRemember: The first ברייתא (בעל חוב takes בינונית) is about a man who had עידית and sold it. The second ברייתא (בעל חוב takes זיבורית) is about a man who never had עידית.

phrases.english: Rather, must we not conclude from this:
here, it is where he had top-quality land and sold it,
phrases.notes: "Here" is the first ברייתא, where the creditor collects from the middle-quality land.

phrases.aramaic: כָּאן – שֶׁלֹּא הָיְתָה לוֹ עִידִּית וּמְכָרָהּ?
phrases.english: there, it is where he did not have top-quality land and sell it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Settles the contradiction from step 5 using רב חסדא's case, which completes the proof.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The contradiction between the two ברייתות goes away only if you split them this way.

steps.title: Another answer: does his בינונית match the world's עידית?
steps.stepSummary: A second way to settle the contradiction. Both ברייתות are about a man who never had עידית. The difference is whether his בינונית is as good as the world's עידית.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or you could say: both are about a man who did not have עידית and sell it. It is still not a problem. This one is where his בינונית is as good as the world's עידית, and that one is where his בינונית is not as good as the world's עידית.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a different way to settle the contradiction, without using רב חסדא's case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If his בינונית is as good as top land anywhere, it counts as עידית, so the בעל חוב goes to the זיבורית (the second ברייתא). If it is only average by the world's standard, it is truly בינונית, and the בעל חוב can take it (the first ברייתא). This means the proof for רב חסדא is not a must.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you want, say...; it introduces another possible answer
Both this one and that one
Is equal to, is as good as
Of the world, meaning land in general

phrases.english: And if you wish, say:

phrases.aramaic: אִידֵּי וְאִידֵּי שֶׁלֹּא הָיְתָה לוֹ עִידִּית וּמְכָרָהּ;
phrases.english: both this and that are where he did not have top-quality land and sell it;
and it is not difficult:
this one is where his middle-quality land is equal
phrases.notes: "This one" is the second ברייתא, where the creditor gets only the poor-quality land.

phrases.english: to the top-quality land of the world,
and here it is where his middle-quality land is not equal
to the top-quality land of the world.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי בָּעֵית אֵימָא אִידֵּי וְאִידֵּי שֶׁלֹּא הָיְתָה לוֹ עִידִּית וּמְכָרָהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different way to settle the contradiction, which weakens the proof from step 6.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases differently: whether his land matches the world's top land.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Only רב חסדא's case (had עידית and sold it) can settle the contradiction.
steps.terutzMaskana: Even if he never had עידית, the ברייתות can differ based on how good his בינונית is by the world's standard.

steps.title: A third answer: the two תנאים disagree about how to grade land
steps.stepSummary: Both ברייתות are about the same case, where his בינונית is average even by the world's standard. The two תנאים disagree on whether to grade his land against his own fields or against fields in the world.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or you could say: both are about a case where his בינונית is like the world's בינונית. Here they disagree about this point. One master holds that we grade by his own land, and the other master holds that we grade by the world's land.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a third answer. The two ברייתות are not talking about different cases. They are two תנאים who disagree.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The one who grades by his own land counts his best field as עידית, so the בעל חוב goes to the זיבורית (the second ברייתא). The one who grades by the world's land calls that field בינונית, so the בעל חוב can take it (the first ברייתא).

keyTerms.meaning: By his own land / by the world's land

steps.whatToRemember: So far there are three ways to settle the two ברייתות: (1) he had עידית and sold it, or he never did; (2) his בינונית matches the world's עידית or it does not; (3) the תנאים disagree whether we grade by his own land or by the world's land. רבינא adds a fourth way in the next step.
steps.confusionAlert: In the first two answers both ברייתות agree on the הלכה and only the cases differ. In this third answer the case is the same, and the ברייתות really disagree.
steps.whyThisMatters: This brings back the big question of the סוגיא: is land graded against the owner's own fields or against fields in the world?

phrases.english: And if you wish, say:

phrases.aramaic: אִידֵּי וְאִידֵּי כְּגוֹן שֶׁהָיְתָה בֵּינוֹנִית שֶׁלּוֹ
phrases.english: both this and that are a case where his middle-quality land was
like the middle-quality land of the world,
and here they disagree about this:
One master holds: they grade by his own land.
phrases.notes: This is the second ברייתא, which sends the creditor to the poor-quality land.

phrases.aramaic: וּמָר סָבַר: בְּשֶׁל עוֹלָם הֵן שָׁמִין.
phrases.english: And the other master holds: they grade by the world's land.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא אִידֵּי וְאִידֵּי כְּגוֹן שֶׁהָיְתָה בֵּינוֹנִית שֶׁלּוֹ כְּבֵינוֹנִית דְּעָלְמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A third way to settle the contradiction: a disagreement between תנאים instead of two different cases.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The two ברייתות must be about different cases.
steps.terutzMaskana: They can be about the same case and simply disagree about whether land is graded by his own fields or by fields in the world.

steps.title: רבינא: The two ברייתות argue about עולא's teaching
steps.stepSummary: רבינא gives a fourth way to settle the contradiction. It is based on עולא's teaching that by Torah law a בעל חוב collects from זיבורית, learned from the פסוק about the pledge brought outside.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said: the two ברייתות disagree about עולא's idea. עולא said: by Torah law, a lender collects from the worst land. The פסוק says: 'Stand outside, and the man you lent to will bring the pledge out to you.' What does a person normally bring outside to give? The worst of his things.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא offers a new answer to the clash between the two ברייתות. He starts by quoting עולא's teaching that by Torah law a lender only gets the worst land.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier answers said the two ברייתות are about different cases, or about how to grade the land. רבינא instead says they disagree about a basic rule. Here he lays the foundation from the פסוק: the borrower hands over what he chooses, and people hand over their worst items. So by Torah law the lender gets זיבורית.

keyTerms.meaning: By Torah law, before any rule the Sages added
The person you lent money to
A pledge or collateral taken for a loan
The worst of a person's belongings

steps.confusionAlert: עולא is not saying the actual practice is to collect from זיבורית. He is only saying what the Torah law is. The very next line explains why the Sages changed it.

phrases.english: Ravina said: they disagree about Ulla's teaching
phrases.notes: "They" means the two ברייתות that seemed to clash.

phrases.english: For Ulla said:
By Torah law, a creditor collects from the poorest-quality land,
as it says: "You shall stand outside,
and the man to whom you lent
will bring the pledge out to you"

phrases.aramaic: מָה דַּרְכּוֹ שֶׁל אָדָם לְהוֹצִיא לַחוּץ –
phrases.english: What does a person usually bring out?
The worst of his belongings.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A fourth answer to the same contradiction, after the answers in steps 6, 7 and 8
steps.terutzResolutionType: Disagreement between the תנאים about a basic rule
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתות must be talking about different cases, or about how to grade the land
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתות disagree about whether the Torah law (זיבורית) or the Sages' later rule applies
steps.mimraCoreRuling: By Torah law, a בעל חוב collects from זיבורית

steps.title: Why the Sages moved the creditor up to middle-grade land
steps.stepSummary: עולא explains that the Sages set up a rule letting a בעל חוב collect from בינונית. They did this so that lenders would not stop lending.
steps.simpleTranslation: So why did the Sages say a lender collects from middle-grade land? So that you won't lock the door in the face of people who need to borrow.
steps.whatsHappening: עולא continues his own teaching. He explains why the actual rule is בינונית even though the Torah law is זיבורית.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If lenders could only take the worst land, they would not want to lend at all. Then people who need loans would be stuck. So the Sages made a תקנה that gives lenders better land, which keeps loans available.

keyTerms.meaning: So why did the Sages say this?
Locking the door, meaning people would stop lending

steps.whyThisMatters: This is a famous principle. The Sages sometimes adjust a Torah-level money rule so that people keep lending and the economy keeps working.

phrases.english: And why did they say
that a creditor collects from intermediate-quality land?

phrases.aramaic: כְּדֵי שֶׁלֹּא תִּנְעוֹל דֶּלֶת בִּפְנֵי לֹוִין.
phrases.english: So that you will not lock the door in the face of borrowers.
phrases.notes: If lenders only got bad land, they'd stop lending, and borrowers would find the door shut.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמָה טַעַם אָמְרוּ בַּעַל חוֹב בְּבֵינוֹנִית
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes עולא's teaching by explaining the Sages' added rule
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The Sages made a rule that a בעל חוב collects from בינונית, so that people will keep lending

steps.title: One תנא follows עולא's enactment, the other does not
steps.stepSummary: רבינא applies עולא's teaching. The ברייתא that says בינונית follows the Sages' rule. The ברייתא that says זיבורית does not accept that rule and stays with Torah law.
steps.simpleTranslation: One master holds by עולא's enactment, and the other master does not hold by עולא's enactment.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא finishes his answer. He shows how עולא's teaching explains the clash between the two ברייתות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first ברייתא, which says the lender collects from בינונית, accepts the Sages' rule. The second ברייתא, which says זיבורית, does not accept that rule, so it stays with the Torah law. Now the two ברייתות are simply two opinions.

keyTerms.meaning: The other master does not hold this view
An enactment or rule set up by the Sages

steps.whatToRemember: There are four answers to the clash between the ברייתות. (1) The cases are different: the man had עידית and sold it, or he never had it. (2) The cases are different: his בינונית is as good as the world's עידית, or it is not. (3) The תנאים disagree whether we grade by his own land (בשלו) or by the world's land (בשל עולם). (4) רבינא: the תנאים disagree about whether to accept the Sages' rule (בינונית) or stay with Torah law (זיבורית).

phrases.english: One master holds by Ulla's enactment,
phrases.notes: This is the תנא of the ברייתא that said בינונית.

phrases.english: and the other master does not hold by Ulla's enactment.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies עולא's teaching to the two ברייתות
steps.terutzResolutionType: The two ברייתות are opposing opinions
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The two ברייתות seem to contradict each other about the same case
steps.terutzMaskana: The בינונית ברייתא accepts the Sages' rule; the זיבורית ברייתא stays with Torah law

steps.title: Selling to one buyer, or to three at once: the buyers take the owner's place
steps.stepSummary: A new ברייתא. If the debtor sold his fields to one person, or to three people at the same time, the buyers simply step into his shoes, and each creditor collects as he would have from the owner.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: if he sold his fields to one person, or to three people at the same time, all of them take the place of the owner.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new ברייתא about a debtor who sold his fields. This line covers a sale to one buyer, or to three buyers at the same time. The גמרא will later ask exactly what the one-buyer case means (steps 14–16).
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each creditor already had a claim on the debtor's land when the debt was created. In these cases the buyers stand in the owner's place, and each creditor collects from the grade of land he would have taken from the owner. For three buyers at once the reason is clear: no sale came first. The one-buyer case is explained later.

keyTerms.meaning: The Rabbis taught; it introduces a ברייתא
They step into the owner's place

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
If he sold to one person
phrases.notes: He is a man who owes several debts and owns good, middle and poor fields, and he sold all of them.

phrases.english: or to three people at the same time,
all of them step into the place of the owner.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: מָכַר לְאֶחָד אוֹ לִשְׁלֹשָׁה בְּנֵי אָדָם כְּאֶחָד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic: collecting from fields that were sold to buyers
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A single buyer of all the fields, or three buyers who bought at the same time, stand in the owner's place for his debts

steps.title: Selling one after another: collect from the last buyer first
steps.stepSummary: If the fields were sold one after the other, all the creditors collect from the last buyer. If he does not have enough, they go to the buyer before him, and then to the one before that.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he sold them one after the other, all the creditors collect from the last buyer. If he doesn't have enough, they collect from the one before him. If he doesn't have enough either, they collect from the one before that.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא continues with the second case: the fields were sold at different times. Now the creditors must go to the most recent buyer first.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A creditor may not take land from a buyer while the debtor still owns enough land to pay. So after each sale, the creditors' claim falls on the land the debtor still has, whatever its grade. That is why the last buyer pays first, no matter how good his field is, and the earlier buyers are only reached if the later ones don't have enough.

keyTerms.meaning: One after the other, at different times
They collect from the last buyer
From the buyer who bought before him

steps.confusionAlert: Here the grade of the land (עידית, בינונית, זיבורית) does not decide anything. Only the order of the sales matters: the last buyer pays first.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the basis of a well-known rule: when a debtor's fields are sold one after another, a creditor collects from the last buyer first and works backward.

phrases.english: If he sold them one after the other,
all of the creditors collect from the last buyer.
If he does not have enough, the creditor collects from the buyer before him;
if he does not have enough either, the creditor collects from the buyer before that one.

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּזֶה אַחַר זֶה – כּוּלָּן גּוֹבִין מִן הָאַחֲרוֹן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The second half of the same ברייתא, giving the case opposite to step 12
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When the fields were sold one after another, creditors collect from the last buyer first, then work backward

steps.title: What case is 'sold to one person'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what situation the ברייתא means when it says the debtor sold his fields to one person.
steps.simpleTranslation: The ברייתא said 'he sold them to one person.' What exactly is the case?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the first case of the ברייתא and asks what kind of sale it means. This question sets up the next steps, which test the possible answers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Selling to one person could happen in two ways. He could sell all the fields in one sale, or he could sell them one at a time. The גמרא wants to know which one the ברייתא means, because the rule might change depending on the answer.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? What are the exact circumstances?
A teaching of the תנאים that is not in the משנה

phrases.english: "He sold them to one person" — what is the case?
phrases.notes: This is quoted from the ברייתא in step 12, where the buyer simply steps into the owner's shoes.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the ברייתא from steps 12 and 13 to pin down the exact case of its first clause.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether 'sold to one person' means one sale of all the fields at once, or several sales one after another.

steps.title: Selling everything at once would be too obvious to teach
steps.stepSummary: If the sale to one person happened all at once, the case would be obvious. The ברייתא already teaches that three buyers at once all step into the owner's shoes.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you say he sold everything at one time, there is a problem. With three buyers at once, you could have argued that one of them came first. Even so, the ברייתא says they all step into the owner's place. So do we really need to be told the same rule about one buyer at once?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries the first possible reading, that everything was sold at one time, and shows why it cannot be right.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The case of three buyers is the harder one. Someone could think one of them bought slightly earlier, and still the ברייתא treats them all the same. If that is true for three buyers, it is surely true for one buyer who bought everything in one sale. So the ברייתא would not need to teach the one-buyer case at all.

keyTerms.meaning: If you will say (a possible reading the גמרא is about to reject)
At one time, all at once
They step into the owner's place and take on his rights
Is it needed? (meaning it is obvious)

phrases.english: If you say it was at one time —
now, with three buyers,
where one could say that one of them came first,
you say they all step into the owner's place;
is it needed to teach 'he sold them to one person'?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests the first possible answer to the question of step 14 and rejects it.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading that 'sold to one person' means one sale of everything at once.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If three buyers at once all step into the owner's shoes, even though one of them may have come first, then one buyer at once surely does too. Teaching it would be pointless.

steps.title: The one-buyer case means sales one after the other
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא concludes that the ברייתא is talking about one buyer who bought the fields one after the other.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it is clear that he sold them to him one after the other.
steps.whatsHappening: Since the 'all at once' reading failed, the גמרא answers its question. The one-buyer case is about sales one after the other.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now the ברייתא has a real חידוש. The same person bought several fields at different times, and the ruling is that he simply steps into the owner's shoes. The order of his purchases does not matter, and creditors collect as they would have from the owner.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather; introduces the correct option after rejecting another

steps.confusionAlert: Usually פְּשִׁיטָא means 'this is obvious, so why teach it?' and starts a challenge. Here it is not a challenge. It just means 'clearly, the case must be…'

phrases.english: Rather, it is clear: it was one after the other.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 14 once step 15 has ruled out the other option.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The one-buyer case in the ברייתא is about fields sold to the same person one after the other.

steps.title: Why are three buyers one after the other different?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא starts to ask why three buyers one after the other are treated differently from one buyer. Its reason for the three-buyer rule is that each earlier buyer can say: 'I left you land to collect from.'
steps.simpleTranslation: So what is different about three buyers? There, each one can say to the creditor: 'I left you a place to collect from.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sets up a challenge. It first explains why, with three buyers one after the other, the creditors go only to the last buyer. This prepares the next line, which will ask why the single buyer cannot make the same claim.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 13, with three buyers one after the other, the creditors must first collect from the last buyer. The reason is that each earlier buyer can say: 'When I bought, the owner still had land left for you, so go collect from that.' Now that the one-buyer case is also one after the other, the גמרא is getting ready to ask why that one buyer cannot argue the same thing.

keyTerms.meaning: I left you a place to collect from: a buyer's claim that the debtor still had land left for the creditor

phrases.english: And what is different about three buyers?
phrases.notes: He means the case of three buyers one after the other, from step 13, where creditors start with the last buyer.

phrases.english: That each and every one says to him:
phrases.notes: 'Him' is the creditor trying to take the buyer's field.

phrases.english: "I left you a place to collect from";

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on step 16, which made the one-buyer case a sale one after the other, and compares it to the three-buyer case of step 13.
steps.kashyaTarget: The difference the ברייתא makes between one buyer one after the other and three buyers one after the other.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The three-buyer rule rests on the claim 'I left you a place to collect from.' This line sets up the next line, which will ask why a single buyer who bought one after the other cannot make that same claim.

steps.title: A single buyer should also be able to say 'I left you land'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes its challenge. A single buyer who bought the fields one after the other should be able to tell each creditor that he left him land to collect from, just as separate buyers can.
steps.simpleTranslation: In this case too, about each field he bought, let the buyer say to the creditor: "I left you a place to collect from!"
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the question it began in Step 17. Why should one buyer who bought the fields one after the other be treated differently from three separate buyers?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Three buyers who bought one after the other can each say, "When I bought, the seller still had land for you." That pushes every creditor onto the last buyer. One buyer who bought one field at a time can make the same claim about each earlier field, so all the creditors should collect only from the last field he bought. So why did the ברייתא say each creditor collects from his normal kind of land?

phrases.english: This case too,
phrases.notes: He means the case of one buyer who bought all the fields one after the other.

phrases.english: about each and every one, let him say to him:
"I left you a place to collect from!"

steps.triggerLanguage: הַאי נָמֵי אַכֹּל חַד וְחַד לֵימָא לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the challenge that Step 17 started.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's ruling that a single buyer who bought one after the other lets each creditor collect from his normal kind of land.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The reason behind the three-buyer rule ('I left you land') applies just as well to one buyer who bought one field at a time.

steps.title: The case is where he bought the best land last
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the ברייתא is talking about a buyer who bought the עידית last. רב ששת says the same thing.
steps.simpleTranslation: What case are we dealing with here? A case where he bought the best land last. And רב ששת also said: a case where he bought the best land last.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by narrowing the case. The buyer bought the best field (עידית) last, and רב ששת gives the same explanation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the buyer used the argument 'I left you land,' every creditor would end up collecting from the last field, which is his best one. He does not want that. So he chooses not to make the claim, and each creditor collects his normal kind of land.

keyTerms.meaning: what case are we dealing with here?

phrases.english: What case are we dealing with here?
A case where he bought the best land last.
And so said רב ששת:
A case where he bought the best land last.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in Step 18 by limiting the case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The buyer should use 'I left you land' and send everyone to the last field.
steps.terutzMaskana: The last field is the עידית, so the buyer prefers not to use that argument.

steps.title: Then let them all collect from the best land
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: if the עידית was bought last, then by the rule of 'I left you land,' all the creditors should collect from it.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, let them all come and collect from the best land!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the answer. Since the best land was bought last, the creditors themselves should insist on collecting from it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The creditors' rights are pushed onto whatever was bought last. If that field is the עידית, every creditor would happily collect from it, even the woman who normally gets only זיבורית. So the buyer's preference should not matter.

phrases.english: If so,
let them all come and collect from the best land!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי הָכִי לֵיתוֹ כּוּלְּהוּ וְלִיגְבּוֹ מֵעִידִּית
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer given in Step 19.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that the buyer bought the עידית last.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the last field is the best one, the creditors would want to collect from it, and the buyer could not stop them.

steps.title: The buyer threatens to return the worst land to the seller
steps.stepSummary: The buyer can tell the creditors: take your normal share, or I will give the זיבורית back to the seller, and then you will all have to collect from it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because he can say to them: "If you stay quiet and take what you are normally entitled to, take it. But if not, I will return the document for the worst land to its owner, and you will all collect from the worst land."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the creditors cannot all grab the עידית. The buyer has a threat he can use against them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: As long as the seller still owns some land, creditors must collect from the seller's land and cannot take from buyers. If the buyer gives the זיבורית back to the seller, the seller owns land again, and all the creditors are stuck with that זיבורית. So the creditors do better by accepting their normal kinds of land.
steps.whatToRemember: A single buyer who bought one field at a time lets each creditor collect his normal kind of land. The reason is that he can threaten to return the worst field to the seller and force everyone onto it.
steps.confusionAlert: Returning the worst field costs the buyer only his least valuable field. It puts land back in the seller's hands, and creditors must collect from the seller's own land before taking from any buyer.

phrases.english: Because he can say to them:
"If you stay quiet and take according to your rights,
phrases.notes: He means each one's normal share: the injured party gets the best land, the lender the middle land, and the woman the worst land.

phrases.english: take it.
But if not,
I will return the document for the worst land to its owner,
phrases.notes: The 'owner' is the seller, the man who owes the money.

phrases.english: and you will all take from the worst land."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in Step 20.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Practical leverage held by the buyer
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The creditors could all insist on the עידית that was bought last.
steps.terutzMaskana: The buyer's threat to return the זיבורית to the seller pushes the creditors to accept their normal shares.

steps.title: If so: setting up a new challenge
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says 'אִי הָכִי', 'if so,' to open a new challenge built on the answer from the last step.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so (if the buyer really can make that threat about returning the זיבורית)...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up its next question. It accepts the last answer for a moment and is about to show what problem that answer causes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The last step said the buyer can protect himself by threatening to give the זיבורית back to the seller. 'אִי הָכִי' means 'if that is true.' The full challenge comes in the next lines, where the גמרא will ask whether this reasoning fits the rest of the ברייתא.

keyTerms.meaning: If so: a phrase that takes the last answer and gets ready to challenge it

steps.confusionAlert: This line is not a full question by itself. It only opens the challenge. Wait for the next lines to see what the problem is.

phrases.english: If so,
phrases.notes: He means: if the buyer really can make that threat about returning the זיבורית, as we just said.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Takes the answer from step 21 (the threat to return the זיבורית to the seller) as its starting point for a new challenge.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer from step 21 that the buyer can threaten to return the זיבורית to the seller.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Setup only: if this reasoning is right, it should lead to results that the ברייתא does not seem to accept. The details come on the next amud.
